Fredrik Gustafsson / Linköping

Find the signal in the noise

Fredrik Gustafsson is a signal professor in the broadest sense: someone who looks for meaningful structure in noisy reality. He likes problems that matter, people he enjoys, challenges that are difficult as hell, and ideas exciting enough to steal time from golf.

He moves between mathematics and field reality with little respect for disciplinary borders, turning uncertain measurements into decisions, research into systems, and occasionally equations into companies.

Nature, competition, family, humour and a portable espresso machine belong to the same story.

Having achieved most of the conventional things he once aimed for, he is now in the fortunate and slightly dangerous position of being free to see what turns up next.

S4 · fyra ess i leken

What makes a problem worth doing?

I see more potentially interesting research problems than I could pursue in several lifetimes. So I need a filter. It has four S's—in Swedish, fyra ess i leken.

Samhällsnytta Societal benefit

Does it matter? Something useful should happen if we succeed. There should be a reason beyond producing another paper.

Socialt People

Do I want to do it with these people? Research consumes too much of life to spend it with people you don't enjoy.

Svårt som fan Difficult as hell

Is it genuinely difficult? If somebody else can easily solve it, they should. I can play golf instead.

Spännande Exciting

Do I actually want to know the answer? This one has to make me curious enough to act.

The world. The people. The problem. Me.

    return

    return
elseif ~svart_som_fan

Ngulia · Tsavo

Occasionally found in trees.

Project Ngulia brought smartphones, sensors, cameras, radar and drones into ranger operations at a Kenyan rhino sanctuary. The objective was never a better gadget. It was a better decision available to the people protecting wildlife.

Field equipment — Trail cameras · Tracking tags · Laptop · Drone · Espresso machine

During the pandemic I once supervised a licentiate defence remotely from a leopard cliff in Tsavo. Connectivity was adequate. The battery-powered espresso machine also worked.

Research, then reality

Occasionally, the equations escape the university

Looking back, the companies are not quite as random as they seem.

I like cars. I like rock'n'roll. I don't like spending more time in shopping malls than necessary. I like animals and nature. And I like ideas that fly.

More importantly, they all started with research problems interesting enough to survive S4.

Then occasionally someone founded a company.

personal attraction → research question → company → concrete consequence → equations

A company is not a departure from research. It is one route by which an idea learns to move without its originator.

1998

Sigmoid

I like new ideas.

My first company, and still my playground for new projects.

SIGnals, MOdels and IDentification.

It also refers to the sigmoid function in neural networks.

And if someone asks rudely enough, I explain that sigmoid is Latin for asshole.

This explanation may not survive consultation with an actual Latin scholar.

2001

NIRA Dynamics

I like cars.

What can a car learn from sensors it already has?

Research on vehicle signal processing, estimation and sensor fusion helped turn that question into NIRA Dynamics.

One result was indirect tyre-pressure monitoring: infer something useful without adding another physical pressure sensor. The same philosophy later expanded from understanding the car to understanding the road.

Show me the equations → F. Gustafsson, “Slip-based tire-road friction estimation,” Automatica, 1997.
2003

Softube

I like rock'n'roll.

Then the equations found a guitar amplifier.

Research on nonlinear system modelling and system identification met people who cared deeply about what amplifiers actually sounded like. Softube grew from that collision of engineering and music.

Today the brand is used by countless professional producers, GRAMMY-winning engineers and artists worldwide.

Same equations. More distortion.

Show me the equations → B. Ninness and F. Gustafsson, “A unifying construction of orthonormal bases for system identification.”
2010

Senion

I don't like spending more time in shopping malls than necessary.

GPS works beautifully until you walk indoors.

Senion grew from research on what radio measurements, wireless networks, motion sensors and sensor fusion can tell us about the position of a mobile device when satellites are no longer useful.

If the phone can hear and feel its environment, can it figure out where it is?

It could.

Show me the equations → F. Gustafsson and F. Gunnarsson, “Mobile positioning using wireless networks.”
2021

Qulinda

I like animals and nature.

Eventually, the signals grew legs.

Qulinda brings positioning, sensors, communications and AI to animals and nature—from livestock in Sweden to wildlife conservation in Africa.

What is happening, where is it happening, and does someone need to know?

Show me the field notes → How the work started in Kenya and continues in Sweden and Africa.
2025

EastWing

I like ideas that fly.

Stay tuned...

For the record.

Professor at Linköping University since 1999, currently Professor of Sensor Informatics. Research in statistical signal processing, sensor fusion, positioning and tracking, with an unfortunate tendency to spread into cars, aircraft, phones, audio, drones and wildlife.

Author of books including Adaptive Filtering and Change Detection and Statistical Sensor Fusion. IEEE Fellow, recipient of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences' Arnberg Prize, and member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Engineering Sciences.
